issue.title: RFC: switch from select() to poll() on all platforms
issue.body:
CVE-2026-117350 prompted me to look into getting rid of select() in favour of using poll() on all platforms.

The main advantages of doing this would be to get rid of our artificially low file descriptor limit, and to use the same (security-critical) logic on our less-tested platforms as on our main platform.

This also allows to get rid of some platform-specific quirks, such as Windows requiring that we register the exception set, therefore subscribing us to be notified of TCP urgent data and causing unwanted behaviour. But this point is in my opinion less salient, as the move would likely trade some platform-specific quirks for some others.

Work to switch over to poll() was started by @pstratem in #14336, which (thankfully) introduced Linux support. MacOS / BSD support was initially part of the PR, but out of an abundance of caution was then left out after @sdaftuar and @jamesob encountered issues in testing an earlier version of the code. Windows support was not included since WSAPoll [was malfunctioning](https://daniel.haxx.se/blog/2012/10/10/wsapoll-is-broken/).

Windows has since fixed WSAPoll in May 2020 (Windows 10 version 2004). BSD always worked. And for macOS, the latest investigation i'm aware of is [that of @jamesob](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/14336#issuecomment-437384408) in #14336. As far as i can tell, the diagnostic that `knote_fdfind` ignores the difference in filter is incorrect, as `kev->filter == kn->kn_filter` is [checked](https://github.com/apple/darwin-xnu/blob/0a798f6738bc1db01281fc08ae024145e84df927/bsd/kern/kern_event.c#L8033) (link to same commit as James' comment). The misbehaviour seems to be instead caused by how the problematic iteration of the PR listed each socket multiple times, and macOS' poll() implementation collides them in the kqueue (i.e. `{fd, POLLIN}` followed by `{fd, POLLERR|POLLHUP}` loses the `POLLIN`) [^1]. I have verified this by running a reproducer on a macOS VM and having an LLM read the sources.

I have extensively tested a poll implementation, and ran probes, on macOS, Windows and BSD VMs. So i'm fairly confident poll() support isn't broken on any of these platforms (anymore). However...

The events reported by poll() sometimes vary depending on the platform, and this is a reason why this is an RFC issue and not a slam-dunk PR. If we are going to refactor the poll() logic to support the different events reported on each platform, we should aim for consistent `WaitMany` reporting across platforms. But what behaviour do we want?

I think there is two consistent positions:
- Fail optimistically. Poll events are only hints. On a read EOF, send whatever we have left before disconnecting. On a write error, read whatever was left in the buffer.
- Fail closed. Disconnect on any reported event that is not plain readiness, as well as on EOF or a read/write error.

The former avoids unnecessarily dropping a potentially useful message to/from a peer. The latter doesn't, but helps avoid getting tricked into reading when we shouldn't (CVE-2026-117350) or waking but not being able to make progress (#36688). Bitcoin Core does not strictly follow either, so we don't benefit from always reading/writing as much as possible, and have also exposed ourselves to the aforementioned bugs.

Our knee jerk reaction after the concerning vulnerability may be to just fail closed everywhere, but we should also consider that we now also use our socket implementation for the HTTP server, for which the opposite behaviour may be preferable (for instance it would make sense to respond to a client that sends a request and closes its side of the connection).

Thoughts?

To assist this discussion, here are tables from my probe comparing the events reported by select() today versus what poll() would report for each of FreeBSD / macOS / Windows. For select(): R/W/E means readfds/writefds/exceptfds comes back set. For poll(): IN/OUT/HUP/ERR are just the POLL suffixes.

### FreeBSD

| Peer did | select() RecvEvent | poll() RecvEvent | select() SendEvent | poll() SendEvent | select() RecvEvent\|SendEvent | poll() RecvEvent\|SendEvent |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| idle | – | – | W | OUT | W | OUT |
| urgent byte | E | – | W | OUT | WE | OUT |
| FIN or graceful close | R | IN | W | OUT | RW | IN OUT |
| RST | R | IN HUP | W | HUP | RW | IN HUP |
| data | R | IN | W | OUT | RW | IN OUT |
| data + urgent byte | RE | IN | W | OUT | RWE | IN OUT |
| data + FIN or graceful close | R | IN | W | OUT | RW | IN OUT |
| data + RST | R | IN HUP | W | HUP | RW | IN HUP |
| failed connect | R | IN HUP | W | HUP | RW | IN HUP |

### macOS

| Peer did | select() RecvEvent | poll() RecvEvent | select() SendEvent | poll() SendEvent | select() RecvEvent\|SendEvent | poll() RecvEvent\|SendEvent |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| idle | – | – | W | OUT | W | OUT |
| urgent byte | E | – | W | OUT | WE | OUT |
| FIN or graceful close | R | IN HUP | W | OUT | RW | IN HUP |
| RST | R | IN HUP | W | HUP | RW | IN HUP |
| data | R | IN | W | OUT | RW | IN OUT |
| data + urgent byte | RE | IN | W | OUT | RWE | IN OUT |
| data + FIN or graceful close | R | IN HUP | W | OUT | RW | IN HUP |
| data + RST | R | IN HUP | W | HUP | RW | IN HUP |
| failed connect | R | IN HUP | W | HUP | RW | IN HUP |

### Windows

Note that on Windows POLLIN corresponds to RDNORM | RDBAND. So requesting POLLIN will ask to be woken up for both events, but checking for a reported POLLIN (`reported_event & POLLIN`) will match when either of the two is set.

| Peer did | select() RecvEvent | poll() RecvEvent | select() SendEvent | poll() SendEvent | select() RecvEvent\|SendEvent | poll() RecvEvent\|SendEvent |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| idle | – | – | W | OUT | W | OUT |
| idle; our send buffer full | – | – | – | – | – | – |
| urgent byte | E | IN | W | OUT | WE | IN OUT |
| urgent byte; our send buffer full | E | IN | – | – | E | IN |
| FIN or graceful close | R | HUP | W | OUT HUP | RW | OUT HUP |
| FIN; our send buffer full | R | HUP | – | HUP | R | HUP |
| RST | R | ERR HUP | W | OUT ERR HUP | RW | OUT ERR HUP |
| data | R | IN | W | OUT | RW | IN OUT |
| data; our send buffer full | R | IN | – | – | R | IN |
| data + urgent byte | RE | IN | W | OUT | RWE | IN OUT |
| data + urgent byte; our send buffer full | RE | IN | – | – | RE | IN |
| data + FIN or graceful close | R | IN HUP | W | OUT HUP | RW | IN OUT HUP |
| data + FIN; our send buffer full | R | IN HUP | – | HUP | R | IN HUP |
| data + RST | R | ERR HUP | W | OUT ERR HUP | RW | OUT ERR HUP |
| failed connect | E | – | – | OUT ERR HUP | E | OUT ERR HUP |


[^1]: For more details, here is the call chain that would lead to the observed issue:
       - Each pollfd becomes a kevent tagged with its array index, and POLLHUP counts as read interest: [`sys_generic.c#L1745-L1758`](https://github.com/apple-oss-distributions/xnu/blob/xnu-12377.121.6/bsd/kern/sys_generic.c#L1745-L1758)
       - The lookup matches on (kqueue, fd, filter), so a second read registration finds the existing filter: [`kern_event.c#L6808-L6811`](https://github.com/apple-oss-distributions/xnu/blob/xnu-12377.121.6/bsd/kern/kern_event.c#L6808-L6811)
       - Re-registering overwrites the filter’s tag with the new entry’s index: [`kern_event.c#L4249-L4253`](https://github.com/apple-oss-distributions/xnu/blob/xnu-12377.121.6/bsd/kern/kern_event.c#L4249-L4253)
       - The result goes to the tagged entry, masked by that entry’s own events: [`sys_generic.c#L1855-L1878`](https://github.com/apple-oss-distributions/xnu/blob/xnu-12377.121.6/bsd/kern/sys_generic.c#L1855-L1878)

events.body:
poll/select essentially must be treated as merely a hint

correctness is important but so is availability
So `poll(POLLIN)` on Windows would wake up and report urgent data? 😒 What about using `poll(POLLRDNORM)` on all platforms? Would that be consistent to ignore urgent data on all platforms?

Yes, substituting `POLLIN` for `POLLRDNORM` everywhere would work. I think the bigger issue here is that macOS with poll() returns HUP on a graceful close (when RecvEvent was requested). Versus the current behaviour, this means that because OUT is masked we won't send one last message to the peer before disconnecting. That's probably acceptable, but coupled with the change to immediately disconnect on error [being discussed](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36688#issuecomment-6528271842) (cc @theuni), this means we would drop whatever the peer sent before closing without reading it. That may be acceptable too, though maybe more for p2p than for http, and that's why i opened this issue: it's not clear to me what behaviour we find acceptable, let alone what behaviour we desire.

~Here's what I had in mind: https://github.com/theuni/bitcoin/commits/net-oob-error/~

~I implemented that before seeing @darosior's chart. I'll take a look tomorrow and see if my approach aligns with that data.~

Edit: that attempt just ended up complicating things, disregard.

Concept ACK. When trying to understand everything that's going on in #36716, it's clear that supporting `select` and `poll` is problematic, as they differ _just enough_ in behavior to be dangerous.

Now that we've used `poll` for Linux for years, and assuming the macos/windows kinks are no longer relevant, I think it makes sense to move forward with nuking `select`. I imagine we can come up with a set of in/out events that works everywhere, but we can always resort to ifdef hacks if we have to.

I've pushed a POC branch on top of #36716 that attempts a minimal changeset to switch to `poll` on all platforms: https://github.com/theuni/bitcoin/tree/net-use-poll-everywhere

It's missing documentation updates and the actual removal of `select`. I just wanted to hack it up while I had all the gnarly details paged back into my brain.

> I've pushed a POC branch on top of https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36716 that attempts a minimal changeset to switch to poll on all platforms: https://github.com/theuni/bitcoin/tree/net-use-poll-everywhere

You use the same bit for `HUPEvent` than for `ErrorEvent`. I know it's a quick PoC, but even without that typo, i think this branch reintroduces the spin on Windows, because Windows treats a `POLLIN` registration as `RDNORM | RDBAND` (as per discussion above), and in your branch `RDBAND` would lead to a recv() that does not progress. This approach also requires each caller to handle a new hang-up event, and i'm pretty sure this introduces busy loops on Windows (which can report HUP alone) in I2P / SOCKS5 and the HTTP server since it is not handled there.

I agree with the approach of 1) having callers check for and disconnect on ErrorEvent and 2) on HUP returning a RecvEvent iff RecvEvent was requested and returning an ErrorEvent otherwise.

I have mixed feelings about adding more special cases that callers need to handle. I'd much rather we have a simple contract "you must check for ErrorEvent and disconnect if it's set", and decide when to return `ErrorEvent` based on what poll() returns in a single place in Sock::Wait(Many), and not leak specific errors to callers in the form of `HupEvent` or `ConnErrorEventFlag`.

Here is what i was experimenting with locally, updated to have callers always disconnect on ErrorEvent, and to return Recv/Error on hang-ups: https://github.com/darosior/bitcoin/tree/2610_ditch_select.

Also, i think #36737 and #36786 are pretty useful in testing the various approaches. Rebasing on top of them checks some invariants and explicit some of the behaviour changes. For instance, here is my own approach rebased on top of the tests, with each behaviour changing commit adapting the related tests: https://github.com/darosior/bitcoin/tree/2610_ditch_select_tests.

> > I've pushed a POC branch on top of [#36716](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36716) that attempts a minimal changeset to switch to poll on all platforms: https://github.com/theuni/bitcoin/tree/net-use-poll-everywhere
> 
> You use the same bit for `HUPEvent` than for `ErrorEvent`.

Heh. Forgot to fix that before I pushed. I should've called this a WIP rather than a POC.

> I know it's a quick PoC, but even without that typo, i think this branch reintroduces the spin on Windows, because Windows treats a `POLLIN` registration as `RDNORM | RDBAND` (as per discussion above), and in your branch `RDBAND` would lead to a recv() that does not progress.

Thanks for taking a look in detail. I had a whole system of hacks trying to get macos/linux synced up with the OOB data, but ultimately mac's impl just refuses to do the right thing, so I just punted on that for later. Windows makes this even more frustrating. I'm starting to wonder if you were right all along about `SO_OOBINLINE`.

> This approach also requires each caller to handle a new hang-up event, and i'm pretty sure this introduces busy loops on Windows (which can report HUP alone) in I2P / SOCKS5 and the HTTP server since it is not handled there.

Probably so, yeah. For now I'm just hacking on the p2p side of things to find an incantation that works. I figured we could just migrate that to the other users when we get one.



> I agree with the approach of 1) having callers check for and disconnect on ErrorEvent and 2) on HUP returning a RecvEvent iff RecvEvent was requested and returning an ErrorEvent otherwise.
> 
> I have mixed feelings about adding more special cases that callers need to handle. I'd much rather we have a simple contract "you must check for ErrorEvent and disconnect if it's set", and decide when to return `ErrorEvent` based on what poll() returns in a single place in Sock::Wait(Many), and not leak specific errors to callers in the form of `HupEvent` or `ConnErrorEventFlag`.

My intention with keeping these separated is to allow buffers to continue to be drained when possible rather than immediately disconnecting (or as a side-effect of a write).  Perhaps you're right and no distinction is necessary, but I've found it helpful to keep them separate while hacking.

> Here is what i was experimenting with locally, updated to have callers always disconnect on ErrorEvent, and to return Recv/Error on hang-ups: https://github.com/darosior/bitcoin/tree/2610_ditch_select.

Thanks, will compare approaches tomorrow.

> But what behaviour do we want?

Isn't the behaviour that we want:

 * wake up for read, but nothing to read: consider read-side closed, stop trying to read (connection closes once we finish writing, or once we timeout on waiting for a ping response?)
 * wake up for write, but writing fails: drop connection (or possibly half-close it on our side to attempt to finish reading)
 * write buffer is not empty, and haven't woken up for write for this peer in `$TIMEOUT` seconds: drop connection

and we only use the poll flags to route to Recv() or Send() (and always route to one or the other or both on wakeup), and it's the result of those functions that determine the actual error condition? ie the only condition we should be checking is "are we able to make progress on each wakeup" with failure to be able to make progress being the error condition that triggers closure.

> I think it makes sense to move forward with nuking select.

+1

If we want to do better than what `poll()` gets us, I think we should be moving to platform specific util/sock implementations. I think that's probably unnecessary if we're a strict about ensuring we always make progress on wakeups though.

> and we only use the poll flags to route to Recv() or Send() (and always route to one or the other or both on wakeup), and it's the result of those functions that determine the actual error condition? ie the only condition we should be checking is "are we able to make progress on each wakeup" with failure to be able to make progress being the error condition that triggers closure.

Yes, with the exception of ErrorEvent, which we can use when an error occurs but we can't make more progress, for instance because receive is paused. At this point i think the next best thing to do is to just disconnect.

So concretely for my branch i think it would mean also returning a RecvEvent when POLLERR is raised (and RecvEvent was requested).

We could consider better supporting half closes after that, but it's not clear to me that the complexity would be worth it. I think the next best thing would be to better support actually processing the message that are read on a drain. I believe currently it's extremely racy:
- First, most of our peers run Core, which never half-closes with shutdown() and doesn't drain before closing a connection it decided to drop. Which means we will only get a FIN if we are lucky (and only get a RST after our next send()), but in most cases we'll get an RST right away. Once the RST is in, any send() fails and we disconnect before reading further, since we send first.
- Second, and that's the big one, the message handler thread must consume any read message between the socket thread's final recv() and it setting `fDisconnect`.

In practice, especially with many peers where cycling over all peers' messages takes longer than cycling over all peers' data to read, i think we are far from reliably processing messages sent right before the connection is closed (especially large messages, which i am quite confident we virtually never process).

I'd like to share one issue i've been discussing with Cory.

On macOS, poll() follows POSIX and treats HUP and OUT as mutually exclusive (see table in OP). Linux does not. On a peer's graceful close, macOS will report HUP while Linux will report IN | OUT. That means on Linux we'd try to send first, whereas on macOS we'd recv() and hit EOF immediately. This was detected by [this test failure](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/36726#issuecomment-7147365338).

There are different ways we could deal with this. I'm currently leaning toward accepting the slight (and harmless) behaviour difference between platforms (it's one of several). Another option could be to try to always report the subset of events that would be reported on all platforms, to minimize platform inconsistencies. The downside would be of course that we start modifying the behaviour on Linux, rather than adapt all platforms to it.

Thoughts?

From the same probe data used in OP, here are tables of events returned by poll() on each platform, depending on the requested events and the state of the peer. Presenting the data like so helps spotting inconsistencies and i think can assist the discussion here.

We ask for POLLRDNORM rather than POLLIN as per my branch and discussions above. A dash means nothing is returned.

<details>
<summary>Requested: RecvEvent (POLLRDNORM)</summary>

| Peer state | Linux | macOS | FreeBSD | Windows |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| idle | – | – | – | – |
| idle; our send buffer full | – | – | – | – |
| data | RDNORM | RDNORM | RDNORM | RDNORM |
| data; our send buffer full | RDNORM | RDNORM | RDNORM | RDNORM |
| FIN / graceful close | RDNORM | RDNORM HUP | RDNORM | HUP |
| FIN; our send buffer full | RDNORM | RDNORM HUP | RDNORM | HUP |
| data + FIN | RDNORM | RDNORM HUP | RDNORM | RDNORM HUP |
| data + FIN; our send buffer full | RDNORM | RDNORM HUP | RDNORM | RDNORM HUP |
| RST | RDNORM ERR HUP | RDNORM HUP | RDNORM HUP | ERR HUP |
| listening, idle | – | – | – | – |
| listening, pending connection | RDNORM | RDNORM | RDNORM | RDNORM |
| connect() in progress | – | – | – | – |
| connect() succeeded | – | – | – | – |
| connect() refused | RDNORM ERR HUP | RDNORM HUP | RDNORM HUP | – |
| closed descriptor | NVAL | NVAL | NVAL | poll error |

</details>

<details>
<summary>Requested: SendEvent (POLLOUT)</summary>

| Peer state | Linux | macOS | FreeBSD | Windows |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| idle | OUT | OUT | OUT | OUT |
| idle; our send buffer full | – | OUT | OUT | – |
| data | OUT | OUT | OUT | OUT |
| data; our send buffer full | – | OUT | OUT | – |
| FIN / graceful close | OUT | OUT | OUT | OUT HUP |
| FIN; our send buffer full | – | OUT | OUT | HUP |
| data + FIN | OUT | OUT | OUT | OUT HUP |
| data + FIN; our send buffer full | – | OUT | OUT | HUP |
| RST | OUT ERR HUP | HUP | HUP | OUT ERR HUP |
| listening, idle | – | – | – | – |
| listening, pending connection | – | – | – | – |
| connect() in progress | OUT | – | – | OUT |
| connect() succeeded | OUT | OUT | OUT | OUT |
| connect() refused | OUT ERR HUP | HUP | HUP | OUT ERR HUP |
| closed descriptor | NVAL | NVAL | NVAL | poll error |

</details>

<details>
<summary>Requested: RecvEvent|SendEvent (POLLRDNORM|POLLOUT)</summary>

| Peer state | Linux | macOS | FreeBSD | Windows |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| idle | OUT | OUT | OUT | OUT |
| idle; our send buffer full | – | OUT | OUT | – |
| data | RDNORM OUT | RDNORM OUT | RDNORM OUT | RDNORM OUT |
| data; our send buffer full | RDNORM | RDNORM OUT | RDNORM OUT | RDNORM |
| FIN / graceful close | RDNORM OUT | RDNORM HUP | RDNORM OUT | OUT HUP |
| FIN; our send buffer full | RDNORM | RDNORM HUP | RDNORM OUT | HUP |
| data + FIN | RDNORM OUT | RDNORM HUP | RDNORM OUT | RDNORM OUT HUP |
| data + FIN; our send buffer full | RDNORM | RDNORM HUP | RDNORM OUT | RDNORM HUP |
| RST | RDNORM OUT ERR HUP | RDNORM HUP | RDNORM HUP | OUT ERR HUP |
| listening, idle | – | – | – | – |
| listening, pending connection | RDNORM | RDNORM | RDNORM | RDNORM |
| connect() in progress | OUT | OUT | – | OUT |
| connect() succeeded | OUT | OUT | OUT | OUT |
| connect() refused | RDNORM OUT ERR HUP | RDNORM HUP | RDNORM HUP | OUT ERR HUP |
| closed descriptor | NVAL | NVAL | NVAL | poll error |

</details>

This makes clear that using the intersection of what's reported on all platforms, although already hacky, is sometimes not even possible as that intersection would be empty. So we would have to use the intersection at the level of our own events, which creates even more complexity.

> We could consider better supporting half closes after that, but it's not clear to me that the complexity would be worth it.

> we should also consider that we now also use our socket implementation for the HTTP server, for which the opposite behaviour may be preferable

I think half closes are only really interesting for http/rpc/rest? Finishing reading what we can on p2p when the other side closes the connection is a nice to have, but shouldn't be relied upon or guaranteed, and doesn't really justify any extra complexity? If you want
to guarantee receipt, you keep the connection fully open, send a ping with a fresh nonce and wait for the corresponding pong.

> * Second, and that's the big one, the message handler thread must consume any read message between the socket thread's final recv() and it setting `fDisconnect`.

I don't think that point makes sense: setting `fDisconnect` should still lead directly to `~Sock()` rather than a half-close -- we don't want any further processing of incoming messages, queued or otherwise, because we set `fDisconnect` on misbehaviour/potential DoS. Could introduce an `fFinishUp` distinct from `fDisconnect` for milder cases where the idea is just to free up a connection slot. But that doesn't seem very valuable -- it would just change where the protocol gets artificially cutoff without really adding any more reliability or saving any significant bandwidth, etc? Might be nice to flush any queued writes, possibly only until `send()` would block? But again, not much benefit.

If we want to support half closing sockets ourselves (for bitcoin-cli HTTPClient?), I think that would be introducing a `Sock::CloseSend()` which would (a) do the half-close, (b) make future `Send()` calls be a no-op or immediate error, and (c) continue handling `Recv()` as normal?

> idle; our send buffer full 	– 	OUT 	OUT 	–

Something seems wrong with your test there -- if we're not able to write ("our send buffer full"), poll shouldn't be returning OUT ("Normal data may be written without blocking." per FreeBSD manpage)?

Otherwise, I think:

  * `revents & NVAL` or poll error; socket is already closed, not sure that shouldn't be an assert failure?
  * `revents & (RDNORM | HUP | ERR)` results in a `RecvEvent` and calling `Recv()`, and stop querying for RDNORM if `Recv()` returns 0 bytes
  * `revents & (OUT | ERR)` results in a `SendEvent` and calling `Send()` and closing the socket if `Send()` errors or accepts 0 bytes

ought to work, provided the "poll(OUT) / FIN; our send buffer full" case only returns "HUP" on windows once, and doesn't busy loop. That would automatically drain on half-close, I believe. It wouldn't necessarily automatically drain the recv buffer on RST (a partial read followed by a send failure would kill the socket), but that seems fine to me.
